readerTitle: Why $130,000 later can be worth less than $100,000 now
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 매각, 소프트웨어 회사의 고객 계약) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 할인율은 정해진 숫자가 아니라 '다른 곳에 쓸 수 있는 기회'와 '돈이 정말 들어올지에 대한 확신'을 반영한 판단이다. 같은 약속도 누가, 언제 하느냐에 따라 오늘의 가치가 크게 달라진다.
misconception: 나중에 받는 금액이 더 크면 더 좋은 거래다. 할인율은 은행 금리처럼 어딘가에 정해져 있는 숫자다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (현재가치 = 미래 금액 ÷ (1 + 할인율)^기간, 할인율과 위험의 관계)

cards.title: Two buyers, one restaurant, and a number nobody wrote down
body: You're selling your restaurant. One buyer offers $100,000 today. Another offers $130,000, paid in three years out of the restaurant's future profits.
$130,000 is the bigger number. Whether it's the better deal depends on a number neither buyer mentioned.

image.label: Two envelopes: $100,000 now, $130,000 in three years
image.brief: 식당 테이블 위에 봉투 두 개. 왼쪽 봉투는 "$100,000 · Today", 오른쪽 봉투는 더 크고 "$130,000 · In 3 years" 라벨, 오른쪽 봉투는 살짝 안개 속에 흐릿하게. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which offer do you take?
body: The second buyer has never run a restaurant. They'll pay you only if the place keeps making money under them. You could put cash from a sale into a safe savings account or pay off your own loans.
How do you compare the two offers?

options.feedback: You gain $30,000 on paper but carry three years of waiting and the risk that a new owner can't pay. Those costs never show up in the headline number.

options.text: Take $100,000. Money today always beats money later
options.feedback: Often true, but not always. If the later payment were safe and much larger, it could be worth more. You need a way to compare, not a rule.

options.text: Shrink the $130,000 by a yearly rate that reflects the risk, then compare
options.feedback: That's the idea in this lesson. With a high rate for an unproven buyer, the later offer comes out below $100,000 today.

cards.title: What $130,000 in three years is worth today
body: The answer depends on the yearly rate you use to shrink future money into today's money. Same promise, four rates:
cards.callout: At 20%, the "bigger" offer is worth about **$25,000 less** than cash today.

image.label: What $130,000 in three years is worth today
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Discount rate
body: A **discount rate** is the yearly rate you use to turn future money into what it's worth today. Divide the future amount by (1 + rate) once for every year you wait.
Think of it as an exchange rate between *later* and *now*. A low rate says future money is almost as good as cash. A high rate says a promise is worth much less than money in hand.

image.label: A dial labeled 'rate' shrinking a stack of future coins
image.brief: 왼쪽에 '3 years later'라고 적힌 큰 동전 더미, 가운데에 'Discount rate' 다이얼, 오른쪽에 '오늘의 가치'로 줄어든 동전 더미. 다이얼을 높일수록 오른쪽 더미가 작아지는 느낌을 화살표로 표현.

cards.title: Two things set the rate.
body: The rate isn't found in a bank. You build it from two questions:
list: **What else could this money do?** If cash today could pay off a 9% loan, waiting costs you at least 9% a year.
**How sure is the payment?** A promise from a shaky buyer deserves a higher rate than one from a reliable one.
cards.callout: Safer and closer cash gets a lower rate. Riskier cash gets a higher one.

cards.title: The rate hits distant money hardest.
body: Doubling the rate barely matters for money due next year. For money due in ten years, it cuts the value by about **58%**. That's why long-term promises are so sensitive to the rate you pick.

cards.title: The rate is a judgment, and easy to bend.
body: Because a few points change the answer so much, people can pick the rate that gives the answer they already want. A seller picks a low one. A buyer picks a high one.
Write down why you chose your rate before you calculate. Then try a higher and a lower rate. If the decision flips, the rate is the real question, not the math.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You sell software. Two customers each want a custom integration and offer **$60,000, paid in two years**. One is a large bank that has paid vendors on time for decades. The other is a startup with eight months of cash left.
How should you value the two offers?

options.text: Treat them the same. It's the same $60,000 on the same date
options.feedback: Same face value, very different odds of being paid. Valuing them equally hides the risk you're actually taking on.

options.text: Use a much higher rate for the startup, and ask it for more upfront
options.feedback: At 8%, the bank's promise is worth about $51,000 today. At 30%, the startup's is worth about $35,500. That gap tells you how much upfront payment to ask for.

options.text: Value the startup's promise at zero and turn it down
options.feedback: Cautious, but a risky payment still has some value. A higher rate or better terms can make the deal work instead of losing it.

cards.title: A future dollar is worth what your rate says it is.
body: The discount rate turns promises into today's money. It rises with what else your cash could do and with the risk that the money won't arrive.
**Try it today:** pick one payment you're expecting a year or more from now. Value it at 8% and at 20%. Would you make the same decision at both?
